prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks rest on one clear idea, Katori's magic-wavelength trap, which lets thousands of neutral atoms be held in an optical lattice without the trap shifting the clock transition. Ye's group then showed what the idea could do: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, long coherence, and the first controlled study of interactions and many-body effects inside a clock. Several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) with Sr, Yb and Hg now agree at that level, and the clocks are compared across continents. That is the kind of reproduction I look for. The clocks resolve gravitational redshift across millimetres, they test whether constants drift, and they are the basis for a possible redefinition of the second. The prize would reward a new way to measure time, not a technology that was already known. I would not call it technologically motivated: the clocks are valued because they let us ask new questions about nature. Katori and Ye are a clean two-person attribution. The 2005 comb prize (Hall and Hansch) and the 2012 ion-trap prize (Wineland and Haroche) are neighbouring recognitions, but neither covers the neutral-atom lattice idea or its realisation.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that this is an extension of precision measurement already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and that it is measurement refinement rather than a discovery that changes our picture of nature. The practical culmination, a redefinition of the second, has not yet happened. Early lattice-clock priority is shared with Lemonde's group at SYRTE and with Ludlow, Hinkley and others at NIST, who are not in the credited names. I also cannot ignore that I work close to this field and know several of the people involved, so I should be suspicious of my own enthusiasm. Finally, the case for quantum-simulation (B014) and moire matter (B003) is that they show nature doing something unexpected, whereas a clock is a measurement that exists because we built it.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B003) first as a pattern in which theory predicted flat bands and nature answered with correlated and superconducting states, and he values observational discoveries from nature.
responses.response: I share the admiration for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and for the 2018 experiments, and B003 is my third choice. My reservations are about maturity and attribution. The mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, and sample-to-sample variation in twist angle is a known issue. The three supplied names also leave out Cao and several other experimental groups who established the correlated states, while the first author of the theory paper is the one most easily dropped. A prize for the moire platform would be defensible in a few years, but the optical lattice clock has the settled physics and the reproduction across laboratories that the moire field is still building. I do not think the theory-then-experiment pattern should outrank a result that many groups already agree on at the 1e-18 level.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks active matter (B006) first for a simple model with universal hydrodynamic behaviour, and also gives topological insulators (B023) and the magic-angle graphene candidate high places, while placing the clocks at rank 7.
responses.response: I agree that Vicsek and Toner-Tu is a beautiful piece of statistical physics, and I recognise the elegance in a minimal model that explains flocks, bacteria and colloids. My difficulty is the one you raise yourself: quantitative tests of the Toner-Tu exponents are limited, and the three-person split of Vicsek, Toner and Ramaswamy leaves out Tu. I can only judge this from outside, so I defer to you on the physics, but I would want to hear which experiment tests the exponents. That is what separates it for me from the clock, where quantitative agreement is routine. On B023 I think the overlap with the 2016 prize and the omission of Zhang and the 3D experimentalists are real problems for a three-name prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first as the clearest new measurement technique, and notes that the redefinition of the second is still pending and that credit may extend to Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and Takamoto.
responses.response: I agree on the central case and on timing. I would add a qualification about the reservations. Takamoto and Katori's 2005 demonstration was the first lattice clock, and the original proposal is Katori's, so the credit for the concept is clear. The question is more whether to also name the SYRTE and NIST contributions, which would take us beyond two names. I would resist that. The citation should be written so that it rewards the invention and its realisation to 1e-18, and the pending redefinition should not be a condition, since a prize for the physics does not need the metrology institutions to finish their process. The point on which I would press you is whether the many-body and interaction-physics aspects of the clock, which Ye's group developed, belong in the citation, because I think they strengthen the case that this is physics and not only engineering.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B043) first for a clean new regime of strong light-matter coupling in a circuit, and gives the lattice clock rank 3 and the optical-lattice simulators rank 4. He flags his own proximity to the field.
responses.response: I appreciate that you flagged your proximity, and I will do the same for atomic physics, which is also my own field. On the merits, circuit QED is clearly important, but I share your worry about overlap with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits, because the committee has just spent a prize on superconducting circuits. I think that makes B043 premature. Where we may differ is on B014: you and I both place the lattice-simulation work high, and I would keep it as my main alternative if the committee decides it wants a many-body discovery instead of a measurement. The allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger is the hardest point, and I think a prize that leaves out the theory proposal of Zoller would be a mistake.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock first as an instrument-driven advance with patient control of systematics, and notes that the ion-clock and comb contributions are largely covered by the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the framing and with the maturity assessment. The one thing I would sharpen is the argument about incrementalism: Katori's contribution is not a refinement of the comb or the ion clock. It is a different idea, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the trap does not perturb the transition, and that is why the number of atoms, and with it the statistical power, increases by orders of magnitude. That answers colleagues who see overlap. I would also ask you, since your own field is astroparticle physics, whether you would defend B035 as strongly if the credited names were limited to two, because I ranked it low mainly on attribution within a large collaboration.

uncertainties: Whether colleagues treat the clocks as a new measurement regime or as an incremental step after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-trap prizes.
Whether relative credit for the early lattice-clock demonstrations (Takamoto and Katori, Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley) should affect the two-name configuration.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait until the redefinition of the second has been decided.
If the committee prefers a many-body discovery, the allocation among Bloch, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger for B014 remains unresolved.
statement.conflict_note: No direct conflict with B024 is apparent from my profile: I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I am a long-time collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with Lund and ETH attosecond groups, which bears on attosecond physics but none of the shortlisted candidates directly. I work in theoretical atomic physics, which is adjacent to the lattice-clock and optical-lattice topics (B024, B014), so I flag this closeness of field as a possible bias, though not a recusal issue.
